content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed guidelines for the prevention and control of HIV infections, as well as for addressing Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) within the healthcare sector. These guidelines are intended to provide strategic information and recommendations to improve the global response to HIV. The designations and presentation of material in the publication do not imply any opinion by WHO regarding the legal status of any country, territory, city, or area, nor do they address the delimitation of borders. Any dotted or dashed lines on maps represent approximate boundaries that may not yet be fully agreed upon. The mention of specific companies or manufacturers’ products does not constitute an endorsement or recommendation by WHO over other similar products not mentioned. Proprietary product names are distinguished by initial capital letters. WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the accuracy of the information contained in the publication. However, the material is distributed without any warranty, either expressed or implied. The responsibility for interpreting and using the material lies with the reader, and WHO shall not be held liable for any damages arising from its use. The guidelines include detailed tables and figures, such as the result chain for the health sector response to HIV, the populations served by the cascade of HIV prevention, care, and treatment, and global indicators for monitoring and evaluating the health sector’s response to HIV. Other topics include disaggregations of HIV health sector data, the schematic of the Spectrum AIDS Impact Model, and frameworks for linking care for adults testing HIV-positive, as well as for TB/HIV co-infection and antiretroviral therapy (ART) cascades. The guidelines also address the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, the cascade of prevention, care, and treatment for children, and conceptual frameworks for viral load measures. Additionally, they provide examples of indicators for non-health outcomes, such as stigma and discrimination, and their impact on successful ART programs. The publication acknowledges the contributions of numerous experts, organizations, and technical working groups from around the world. These include representatives from ministries of health, international organizations, academic institutions, and non-governmental organizations. Their expertise and input have been instrumental in shaping the consolidated strategic information guidelines for HIV in the health sector. The guidelines emphasize the importance of collecting and using strategic information to achieve accountability and meet the 90–90–90 targets, which aim to ensure that 90% of people living with HIV know their status, 90% of those diagnosed receive sustained ART, and 90% of those on ART achieve viral suppression. The document also highlights the need for reviewing health and other outcomes, building strategic information capacity, and transforming data into actionable evidence for decision-makers. The publication includes acknowledgments of the technical consultation participants and working groups who contributed to the development of the guidelines. These individuals and organizations represent a wide range of expertise and geographic regions, reflecting the global nature of the HIV response.
